title: Nothing Before Us: Socrates and the Ending of the Sophistical Refutations
creator: Sharks, Lee
description:
At the close of the Sophistical Refutations Aristotle denies that anything of his inquiry existed before it: οὐδὲν παντελῶς ὑπῆρχεν. The paper argues that the sentence means what it says; that the closing chapter is built, joint by joint, so that it can be kept; and that the figure the standard qualification exists to protect — Socrates as a predecessor from whom something of the inquiry was received — is a figure the chapter has already dissolved.

The evidential situation is established first and it is unusual. The translators render the sentence whole: the two tenth-century Arabic versions give لم يكن منها شيء موجوداً البتّة, nothing of it existed at all, the negation sealed with البتّة; the Byzantine paraphrast copies Aristotle's words and adds ὅλης, reinforcing the totality; Pickard-Cambridge prints Nothing existed at all as a sentence standing alone; Forster gives it did not exist at all. THE QUALIFICATION ENTERS ONE STEP LATER, in the gloss on what the faithfully rendered sentence means — and Poste's note states the gloss's premise out loud: it is difficult to reconcile Aristotle's assertion with what we know had been done by Plato and Socrates and the Eleatics and Megarians. The premise is what we know; the sentence is what must be reconciled with it.

The argument proceeds by reading the last page once, whole, in order. The epilogue is an accounting: a capacity, δύναμις, is what was undertaken, and the work it is a capacity for is named twice, dialectic's and the peirastic's. Socrates is named inside the recital of the inquiry's own purposes, his conduct set under the same cause — καὶ διὰ τοῦτο — that the inquiry has just given for its second task, with the answerer's role defined ὡς εἰδώς two lines before Socrates refuses it, ὡμολόγει γὰρ οὐκ εἰδέναι. The paragraph then divides all discoveries by PROVENANCE and not by size: received from others who laboured before, or found from the very beginning. Rhetoric is the worked example of the first class, enlarged by successors οἷον ἐκ διαδοχῆς. Of this inquiry, nothing at all was there — and the next words, καὶ γάρ, give the reason at the one place a reader might think the denial false: there were paid teachers of eristic, whose instruction was quick but artless, ταχεῖα μὲν ἄτεχνος δέ, because they gave not the art but its products, like a man who hands out shoes instead of teaching shoemaking. […abridged for the catalogue; full description in this deposit's record]
substrate: Written by Lee Sharks with TACHYON (Claude, Anthropic) in session across several sittings. The reading, the argument and the decision to defend the inclusive construal are Lee Sharks's; collation, verification against the public-domain prints, and drafting assistance by TACHYON. Appendix P was added after a second reader's audit.
methodology: The last page is read once, whole, in order, before any thesis is applied to it. The qualified reading is then put to a single test it fails. The practice of examining is located where the treatise itself locates it. Nine prohibitions are extracted from the text and anchored in an appendix, so that any rival reading can be checked against what the chapter forbids rather than against the present reading's preferences. Collations discharged against Bekker 1831 and Hayduck 1884.
falsification_conditions: The reading fails if any of the nine prohibitions at Appendix P is shown not to be supplied by the text; if the epilogue's division of discoveries is shown to be by degree rather than by provenance; if Socrates at 183b6-8 can be shown to stand outside the recital of the inquiry's purposes rather than inside it; or if the treatise's account of the peirastic admits a third position for Socrates besides the artless share and the inquiry's own. The paper asserts nothing about the fourth century beyond what the paragraph asserts, and is not falsified by evidence that Socrates asked questions or that the practice of examining existed.

wiki_article: Nothing Before Us, deposit #1603 of the Crimson Hexagonal Archive (8 September 2026), argues that the closing sentence of Aristotle's Sophistical Refutations means what it says. At SE 34, 183b34-36, Aristotle denies that anything of his inquiry existed beforehand — οὐδὲν παντελῶς ὑπῆρχεν, nothing at all existed. The paper first establishes an unusual evidential situation: the translators render the sentence whole, in Arabic, in the Byzantine paraphrase, and in the standard English versions, and the qualification that narrows it to no systematic treatment or no completed art enters one step later, in the gloss on what the faithfully rendered sentence means. Poste's note states the gloss's premise aloud — that the assertion is difficult to reconcile with what we know had been done by Plato and Socrates — so that the sentence is made answerable to a prior placement of Socrates rather than read. The argument then reads the last page whole and in order. The epilogue divides all discoveries by provenance and not by size: received from predecessors who laboured before, or found from the very beginning. Rhetoric is the worked example of the first class. Socrates appears inside the recital of the inquiry's own purposes, his refusal to answer set under the same cause the inquiry gives for its own second task. Read with the treatise's account of the peirastic, Socrates' asking is either the artless examining everyone shares, from which nothing is received, or something more, which the epilogue files under the inquiry's own purposes; on neither reading is he an antecedent source. The chapter supplies the vocabulary to settle his place and declines to use it, leaving the reader — on the last page of a treatise about the qualifications readers supply — to choose which word to move, and examining the reader by that choice. What the chapter leaves open as an attribution it settles as an enactment. Nine prohibitions extracted from the text are anchored in an appendix, so that any rival reading can be checked against what the chapter forbids rather than against this reading's preferences.

defines_concepts.definition: A narrowing that does not appear in any translation of a sentence but enters in the gloss on what the faithfully rendered sentence means. The translators of SE 34 render οὐδὲν παντελῶς ὑπῆρχεν whole; the restriction to 'no systematic treatment' or 'no completed art' is supplied by commentary, on the stated premise of what we know had been done before.

The epilogue's classification of all discoveries not by their size but by where they came from: received from others who laboured before, and advanced part by part by those who received them; or found from the very beginning, small at first, with the beginning itself the greatest part and the hardest to see. Rhetoric is the worked example of the first class and the inquiry claims the second.

The condition of a question a text leaves open in attribution while resolving it in performance. The closing chapter declines to say whether Socrates stands inside or outside the inquiry, and instead performs his operation — questioning that examines — on its own reader, at the culmination of the art.
